questions.q: What is the book's main argument about corporate apologies?
a: Constant apologizing drains the word of its meaning
Companies apologize far too rarely to customers
Apologies should always be made in writing
Customers prefer apologies to refunds
questions.why: Lesson 1 uses American Airlines' roughly 200 daily apologies as an example.

questions.q: What does the Tesco example show?
a: Using the same words for grave and trivial errors weakens them
Apologizing quickly prevents public backlash
Companies should never admit fault online
Compensation matters more than wording
questions.why: Lesson 1 contrasts a medication error with a costume labeling mistake.

questions.q: Why did Zuckerberg's second privacy apology feel hollow?
a: He was apologizing again for the same problem
He refused to appear in public
He blamed users for sharing data
He offered no compensation to anyone
questions.why: Lesson 2 says apologies lose trust when nothing changes afterward.

questions.q: What did JetBlue's CEO do after major disruptions?
a: He apologized and published a customer bill of rights
He offered free flights to every customer
He fired the staff responsible
He waited for the anger to fade
questions.why: Lesson 2 presents the action plan as the model for a real apology.

questions.q: When does the summary say silence may be the best response?
a: When you are not at fault and the noise will pass
When you want to avoid legal responsibility
When customers are clearly in the right
When a competitor is watching closely
questions.why: Lesson 3 compares it to letting muddy water settle on its own.
